hints: Focus on what changes the position of the ammonia equilibrium, think about pressure and removing a reactant.
Opening tap 1 lets the gases expand into an evacuated vessel, so total pressure falls and the equilibrium favours the side with more gas moles.
Lithium removes nitrogen as solid Li3N, so the ammonia system must break down ammonia to replace the lost nitrogen.
walkthrough:
**Write down the two key reactions**

Think like a detective. There is the reversible equilibrium in the middle, and a possible irreversible side reaction on the right.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$$
$$6\text{Li}(\text{s}) + \text{N}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{Li}_3\text{N}(\text{s})$$

**What happens if you open tap 1?**

The middle gases expand into the evacuated left vessel. Volume goes up, so partial pressures and total pressure go down.

By Le Chatelier, lower pressure favours more gas moles. Left side has 4 moles, right side has 2 moles, so equilibrium shifts left and ammonia is used up.

**What happens if you open tap 2?**

Nitrogen can now reach the lithium and is permanently removed as solid $\text{Li}_3\text{N}$.

Removing $\text{N}_2$, a reactant of the ammonia equilibrium, pulls the equilibrium to the left to try to replace it: $$2\text{NH}_3(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g})$$ So ammonia decreases again.

**Compare all actions**

Keeping taps closed causes no disturbance, so no shift left occurs. Opening tap 1 only causes a pressure shift left. Opening tap 2 only causes a concentration shift left. Opening both causes both losses.

Therefore doing nothing preserves the most ammonia.

options.A: With both taps closed the middle vessel stays isolated at its original equilibrium volume and composition. No pressure drop and no loss of N2 to lithium occurs, so no left shift is triggered and ammonia amount stays highest.
options.B: This combines both harmful effects. Expansion into the left vessel lowers pressure and shifts equilibrium left, while contact with Li removes N2 and shifts equilibrium left further. This gives the least ammonia, not the most.
options.C: Opening to the evacuated vessel doubles the available volume for the gases. Lower pressure favours the 4-mole side (N2 + 3H2) over the 2-mole side (2NH3), so ammonia dissociates and its amount falls.
options.D: Li reacts with N2 to make solid Li3N, removing N2 from the gas mixture. By Le Chatelier, the ammonia equilibrium shifts backward to make more N2, which consumes NH3. Students sometimes think removing N2 drives forward reaction, but removal of a reactant drives the reverse reaction.
